newsitem.title: PERU: Peru embassy attackers thought defeated in 1992.
newsitem.headline: Peru embassy attackers thought defeated in 1992.

text.p: The little-known guerrilla group that stormed the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima on Tuesday was believed to have been defeated in 1992 when its leader and his top lieutenant were captured.
After the capture of its leader Victor Polay in June 1992, the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA), named for an 18th century rebel leader who fought Spanish colonisers, kept a low profile.

It was only in January of this year that it burst into the headlines again when an American, Lori Berenson, was convicted by a Peruvian military court of helping plot a takeover of Peru's Congress by the Cuban-inspired MRTA and sentenced to life imprisonment.
The court's verdict was based on accusations that Berenson, 27, transported arms, helped to psychologically prepare MRTA fighters and gathered intelligence by posing as a magazine journalist.
Founded in Lima in 1984, the group was believed to have between 300 and 600 members and operate mainly in the upper Huallaga Valley, in eastern Peru, an area infested with drug smugglers.

The more powerful Maoist Shining Path guerrilla movement considers the MRTA a traitor to Communism and the two groups are reported to have clashed repeatedly for taxes from cocaine smugglers in the Huallaga.
At its peak the MRTA attacked Western embassies, robbed banks, kidnapped business executives and bombed fast-food restaurants. Supporters said it stole from the rich to help the poor.
The latest incident came at a time when President Alberto Fujimori claimed victory over terrorism in Peru, a poor Andean country that is undergoing economic revitalisation.
More than 30,000 people, mostly civilians killed by soldiers and revels, have died in the fighting since the early 1980s.
The government says it has jailed more than 8,000 rebels belonging to the MRTA and the Maoist Shining Path organisation in that period.
